enhanced.fullText:
The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 (OSH Act), codified at 29 U.S.C. §§ 651-678, establishes comprehensive workplace safety standards that apply to higher education institutions as employers. The Act empowers the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) to enforce safety standards and requires employers to maintain safe working environments for all employees, including faculty, staff, and student workers.

Under 29 U.S.C. § 654(a)(1), universities have a general duty to provide workplaces "free from recognized hazards" that could cause death or serious physical harm. This encompasses all campus facilities, including laboratories, maintenance areas, residence halls, dining facilities, and administrative buildings. The specific emergency action plan requirement stems from 29 CFR § 1910.38, which mandates written emergency procedures for workplaces with more than 10 employees.

Key provisions affecting higher education include laboratory safety standards under 29 CFR § 1910.1450 (Laboratory Standard), which requires chemical hygiene plans and designated safety officers for facilities using hazardous chemicals. Universities must also comply with bloodborne pathogen standards (29 CFR § 1910.1030) in medical facilities, research labs, and health centers, requiring exposure control plans and employee training.

The emergency action plan must detail procedures for reporting fires and emergencies, evacuation routes and procedures, critical plant operations shutdown procedures, and designation of responsible personnel. Plans must be reviewed with employees initially and whenever changes occur, as specified in 29 CFR § 1910.38(f).

Enforcement occurs through OSHA inspections, which may be triggered by employee complaints, accidents, or routine compliance checks. Violations are classified as de minimis, other-than-serious, serious, willful, or repeat offenses. Penalties range from $0 for de minimis violations to $156,259 per willful or repeat violation under current adjustment levels (29 U.S.C. § 666). Universities may contest citations through the Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission.

Recent updates include increased penalty amounts adjusted annually for inflation per the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act, and enhanced focus on COVID-19 workplace safety guidance. The Act's coverage extends to student employees and work-study participants, making compliance critical for protecting the entire campus community while avoiding substantial financial penalties and legal liability.
enhanced.summary: The OSH Act requires higher education institutions to maintain safe workplaces through written emergency action plans, hazard elimination, and compliance with OSHA standards, with penalties up to $156,259 per violation.
enhanced.requirements:
## Emergency Action Plan Development
- Develop comprehensive written emergency action plan per 29 CFR § 1910.38
- Include evacuation procedures, alarm systems, and designated assembly points
- Identify emergency response team members and their responsibilities
- Review and update plans annually or when workplace changes occur

## Laboratory Safety Compliance
- Implement chemical hygiene plans under 29 CFR § 1910.1450
- Designate qualified chemical hygiene officers for each facility
- Provide specialized training for laboratory personnel
- Maintain safety data sheets and hazardous chemical inventories

## Training and Documentation
- Conduct initial emergency action plan training for all employees
- Provide refresher training when plans are updated
- Document all training sessions and maintain employee records
- Ensure plans are accessible to employees upon request

## Hazard Assessment and Mitigation
- Conduct regular workplace inspections to identify safety hazards
- Implement corrective measures for identified risks
- Maintain injury and illness logs per 29 CFR § 1904
- Report workplace fatalities and hospitalizations within required timeframes
enhanced.reportingRequirements: Report workplace fatalities within 8 hours and hospitalizations of three or more employees within 24 hours to local OSHA office per 29 U.S.C. § 657(c). Submit annual Form 300A summary of work-related injuries and illnesses by February 1st. Post OSHA citations immediately upon receipt and maintain for three working days or until violation is corrected.
